senses: Having long, attractive legs; long-legged.
Having numerous legs.
Taller or longer than usual.
ety: From leg + -y.
examples: Plants grow leggy if deprived of light.

senses: The individual in a graduating class who delivers the farewell or valedictory address, often the person who graduates with the highest grades.
The individual in a graduating class who graduates with the highest grades.
ety: Formed 1759, from valedictory (“of a speech made when leaving”) + -an.
examples: Our oldest son was valedictorian of his high school class and went to a top university. But right about this time two years ago, our second son told us he wasn’t interested in college.
A social media firestorm erupted last week after two Texas high school valedictorians revealed that they were undocumented immigrants heading to well-respected U.S. colleges with financial aid.

senses: A type of short, buttonless jacket or blouse, open or tied in front and ending at the diaphragm.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish bolero, from bola + -ero. First attested in 1787 (noun). First attested in 1834 (verb).
examples: He took the bolero, which was made of soft angora, and rubbed it up and down his cheek.

senses: A fermented milk drink from the Caucasus and Eastern Europe, similar to yogurt but more liquid.
ety: Borrowed from Russian кефи́р (kefír); see that entry for more.
examples: Water kefir grains differ from milk kefir grains and are generally used to make kefirs based on fruit juices or sugared waters.
Mason jars are great for making kefirs.
Commercially made kefirs on the other hand have seen the development of starter cultures that make the whole process more efficient and quicker while also providing longer product shelf lives.

senses: An unlicensed drinking establishment, especially in Ireland, Scotland, and South Africa.
ety: Borrowed from Irish síbín.
examples: On almost every corner there were shebeens, illegal saloons that were shacks where home-brewed beer was served.
Every night and day there were bombs and gunshots and riots and roundups, and it didn't take long to gain access to the bars and shebeens where these things were discussed with a certain knowingness.

senses: A robotic vacuum cleaner.
ety: Genericized trademark owned by iRobot Corporation. Possibly a blend of room + rumba.
examples: That's so cute... I feel like roomba companies should start implementing cute AIs in the robots that bark or so cute stuff, their sales would skyrocket
Roomba companies after inventing Chloe: It's real free estate
I have an offbrand roomba too, you don't need to actually have the roomba brand in this case; the off brands work just as well sometimes better

senses: An unstressed note or notes before the first strong beat (or downbeat) of a phrase.
ety: Via New Latin from Ancient Greek ἀνάκρουσις (anákrousis, “pushing up”), from ἀνακρούω (anakroúō, “I push up”), from ἀνά (aná, “up”) + κρούω (kroúō, “I strike”).
examples: Then Etheridge poised his baton, jerked an upbeat, and made the violinists speak the low G and A of their anacrusis.

senses: To concentrate toward the essence by making more close, compact, or dense, thereby decreasing size or volume.
ety: Borrowed from Middle French condenser, from Latin condēnsō.
examples: An abridged dictionary can be further condensed to pocket size.
Boiling off water condenses a thin sauce into a soupier mixture.
In what shape they choose, Dilated or condensed, bright or obscure.

senses: The point of junction between two things, in particular a support, that abuts.
Something that abuts, or on which something abuts.
The state of abutting.
That element that shares a common boundary or surface with its neighbor.
A fixed point or surface where resistance is obtained.
ety: First attested in 1644; engineering sense first attested in 1793. From Old French aboutement. Equivalent to abut + -ment.
examples: The fulcrum acted as an abutment.

senses: Dried roots of these plants, or a flavoring material extracted from these roots.
A beverage (soft drink) flavored with this root, such as root beer.
ety: From Spanish zarzaparrilla. The first element may ultimately derive from Basque; see Spanish zarza (“blackberry bush”) for more. The usual pronunciation of the first part of the word as /sæsp-/ or /sɑːsp-/ may be due to dissimilatory loss of the first of two r sounds (compare governor /ˈɡʌvənɚ/ and February /ˈfɛb.juˌɛɹi/). Occasionally this word is pronounced with a schwa between the s and the p, or without a schwa between the p and the r.
examples: Many root teas taste delightful and the old American drink, sarsaparilla, was made on the lines of a decoction, while its pleasant taste was known by most of Victorian Britain.
Say, friend, you got any more of that good sarsaparilla?

senses: A body-length pillow, originating in Japan, which can be embraced or wrapped around one's body while sleeping.
ety: From Japanese 抱き枕 (dakimakura), from 抱き (daki, “to embrace or cling”) + 枕 (makura, “pillow”).
examples: I would follow that up with: "And then they raided his room at his parents' house where they found a Sailor Moon dakimakura and posters of Morning Musume plastering the walls" ...
These character-print dakimakura came into existence in the late '90s as a way for animé fans to get up close and personal with their cartoon sweethearts.
Jin has fallen head over heels for a Japanese 'dakimakura' - or hugging pillow - showing a life sized cartoon of his favourite sexy anime cartoon character Fate Testarossa.

senses: A wall of icons between the sanctuary and the nave in an Eastern Orthodox church.
ety: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek εἰκονόστασις (eikonóstasis), from εἰκών (eikṓn, “icon”) + στάσις (stásis, “fixture”).
examples: The altar was hidden behind an Iconostasis. The church was looked after by an old sacristan who lived in a cottage on the shore of the lake.

senses: The state of being objective; objectivity.
Moral objectivism.
Any of several doctrines that holds that all of reality is objective and exists outside of the mind.
The specific objectivist philosophy created by novelist and philosopher Ayn Rand, endorsing logical reasoning and self-interest.
ety: From objectiv(e) + -ism. First attested in 1854.
examples: First of all, I do not call it Randism; and I don’t like that name. I call it Objectivism, meaning a philosophy based on objective reality. Now let me explain it as briefly as I can.
Into philosophy but not computer games? Then you probably missed Ayn Rand’s objectivism in BioShock (where the villain builds an undersea city out of the reach of government).
But for some, objectivism stuck. Perhaps her most significant early follower was Alan Greenspan, later to serve as chairman of the US Federal Reserve for 19 years.

senses: To come down from a superior position and do something; to deign; (with a negative connotation) to stoop.
To treat someone as though inferior; to talk down to someone; to patronize.
Chiefly followed by on or upon: to go into detail; to particularize, to specify.
ety: From Middle English condescenden, condescendre (“to deign, condescend; to accede graciously; to agree; to agree to, give consent; to make a concession, yield; etc.”), from Old French condescendre (“to descend, go down; to agree or assent to”) (modern French condescendre), from Ecclesiastical Latin condēscendere, the present active infinitive of condēscendō (“to stoop down; to condescend”), from Latin con- (prefix denoting a bringing together of several objects) + dēscendō (“to come or go down, descend; to stoop down”) (from dē- (prefix denoting reversal or undoing) + scandō (“to ascend, mount;
examples: The boss condescended not to sack him after much persuasion from his coworkers.
But she is perfectly amiable, and often condescends to drive by my humble abode in her little phaeton and ponies.
Fanny and little Harriet he seldom condescended to notice; but Mary Ann was something of a favourite.

senses: Hunting, sport; a hunting expedition.
ety: From Urdu شکار / Hindi शिकार (śikār), from Classical Persian شکار (šikār).
examples: Where other men took ten days to the Hills, Strickland took leave for what he called shikar, put on the disguise that appealed to him at the time, stepped down into the brown crowd, and was swallowed up for a while.
They climbed up the ladder, and he mounted shikar fashion, treading first on the sharp edge of the heel and then into the looped-up tail.

senses: headlong; falling steeply or vertically.
Very steep; precipitous.
With a hasty impulse; hurried; headstrong.
Moving with excessive speed or haste; overly hasty.
Performed very rapidly or abruptly.
ety: From Latin praecipitātus (see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more).
examples: When the full stores their ancient bounds disdain, / Precipitate the furious torrent flows.
The king was too precipitate in declaring war.
Being a trifle precipitate in his entry, he trod on a bottle, and was instantly extinguished by a Japanese screen, which appeared to collapse on him out of pure decrepitude.

senses: To punish or reprimand someone severely.
To execrate or condemn something in a harsh manner, especially by public criticism.
ety: First attested in the beginning of the 17ᵗʰ century; borrowed from Latin castīgātus, perfect passive participle of castīgō (“to reprove”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from castus (“pure, chaste”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱes- (“to cut”). Doublet of chastise and chasten, taken through Old French. See also chaste.
examples: Perhaps disarmed by his own scandalous behaviour with Bathsheba, he was in no position to castigate his son for a similar fault.

The curse of avarice and cupidity / Is all my sermon, for it frees the pelf. / Out come the pence, and specially for myself, / For my exclusive purpose is to win / And not at all to castigate their sin.

But despite all this, for Barkan, the universalist notion of an 'Ottoman feudalism' was anathema: he castigated this idea as the concentrated expression of the anti-Ottomanism of the Kemalist Enlightenment.

senses: A varying measure of capacity, usually being a quarter of a barrel; specifically, a measure equal to nine imperial gallons.
A small wooden vessel or cask of indeterminate size, used for butter, lard, etc.
A measurement for the mass of butter, equalling 56 pounds.
ety: From Middle Dutch *vierdekijn, diminutive of vierde (“fourth”), from vier (“four”); equivalent to fourth + -kin.
examples: Barrels came in firkins, nine gallons; kilderkins, eighteen gallons; halves, twenty-seven gallons; barrels, thirty-six gallons and hogsheads, fifty-four.

senses: A beanfeast; any noisy celebration, a party.
Any home-made gas or indigestion remedy.
ety: Clipping of beanfeast + -o.
examples: You gas like a kid at a Sunday School beano.

senses: Someone (or something) doomed; a hopeless case, especially someone who is bound to die soon.
ety: From gone + -er. First attestations around 1850.
examples: I'm a goner if this plan doesn't work.
You'll be a goner if I hit you with this gun.
The sergeant was a goner. There was only one way to save him, and he threw himself on top, hurling the man to the ground.

senses: Having many angles; hence characteristic of a polygon.
Comprised of polygons.
ety: From polygon + -al.
examples: Various forms of conductors have been invented, such as wooden and iron pipes, of a round, square, and polygonal section; but at present, scarcely any other than sheet or cast iron pipes are employed.
The old path paved with polygonal masonry.

senses: A tool used to scour, usually used to clean cookware.
ety: From Middle English scourer, skourer, scowrrere, equivalent to scour + -er.
examples: A scourer may be in the form of a mesh (ball) of wires, a flat piece of a rough fabric, or a pad with a soft sponge-like side and a more abrasive side.

senses: Designating a kind of elaborate ceremonial seat inlaid with ivory, used by the highest magistrates in ancient Rome.
ety: From Latin curūlis (“of or pertaining to a chariot; curule chair”), from currus (“chariot”), from currō (“run”).
examples: Followed by his foolish followers Titus Vinius, who had served him in Spain, Cornelius Laco, an arrogant idiot, and the freedman Icelus Marcianus, who was after Laco’s post, he made for the curule chair.

senses: To cause (something) to become more glad.
ety: From glad + -en.
examples: A balmy night! and tho' the stars be dim, / Yet let us think upon the vernal showers / That gladden the green earth, and we shall find / A pleasure in the dimness of the stars.

senses: The spirit of the age; the taste, outlook, and spirit characteristic of a period.
ety: Unadapted borrowing from German Zeitgeist (literally “spirit of the age”).
examples: After quickly summarizing the zeitgeisten of the Greek, Elizabethan, and early modern periods and their effects on the theatre, Rice turns to the contemporary world.

The vote also stoked fears that Swiss citizens were reflecting the zeitgeist across Europe, where right-wing populists increasingly are seizing the spotlight with an anti-immigration political agenda.

senses: Out of order; not working.
ety: Borrowed from German kaputt (“broken, out of order”), from French capot (“to be without a trick in the card game Piquet”). Cognate to Dutch kapot. Doublet of capot and capote.
examples: Many Trump voters, in other words, have had it. At this point, it seems safe to declare that the historic coalition that powered the president’s second reelection is finished—kaput.

senses: An affectionate or ironic term of address.
ety: From butter + cup. Both sense 1 and 2 are from the flowers' association with butter, from their yellow colour. Compare butterflower for a similar derivation; outside of English, compare Dutch boterbloem, German Butterblume.
examples: When she touched my hand, what a chill I got Her lips are like a volcano that's hot I'm proud to say that she's my buttercup. I'm in love - I'm all shook up.
Listen, buttercup, you're damned good in bed. They don't come any better, but I'm really not interested in playing second fiddle to your camera or your young lovers.

senses: The allowance of something not explicitly approved; tolerance, forbearance.
Specifically, the allowance by a government (or other ruling power) of the exercise of religion beyond the state established faith.
ety: From Middle French toleration, from Latin tolerātiōnem, accusative singular of tolerātiō, from the verb tolerō (“to tolerate”). Compare tolerance.
examples: Above all, the establishment of toleration helped to weaken the presumption that plurality in matters of faith inevitably caused social disorder.

senses: An appellate court of the Spanish empire.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish audiencia. Doublet of audience.
examples: After Cortés the government of New Spain degenerated under the rule of Nuño de Guzmán, president of the first audiencia, into a brutish exploitation of the Indians.

senses: Characterized by plink sounds.
ety: From plink (“to make a plink sound”, verb) + -y (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘having the quality of’).
examples: On Saturday the band members laid down a series of playful indie-rock grooves: plinky keyboards and spidery guitar lines, rattling drums and nudging bass.

senses: That serves to extract something
That withdraws natural resources by extraction
Able to be extracted
ety: From extract + -ive.
examples: Certain branches of industry are conveniently designated extractive: e.g., agriculture, pastoral and mining pursuits, cutting of lumber, etc.

The extractive industry consists of any operations that remove metals, mineral and aggregates from the earth. Examples of extractive processes include oil and gas extraction, mining, dredging and quarrying.
Thirty grains of extractive matter.

senses: The district within which a bailie or bailiff has jurisdiction.
A person's concern or sphere of operations, their area of skill or authority.
ety: From bailie (“bailiff”) and wick (“dwelling”), from Old English wīc.
examples: I established the fairly well-understood pattern that affairs of state were not in my bailiwick.

Jack is full of these insights, thoughtful turns of phrase from a character whose perpetual struggle between wastrel and righteous is all too familiar a bailiwick for the universal insecurities of the human condition.
This “feminist chortling” (as she calls it) about the disgraced royal is right in the bailiwick of the writer who virtually invented the term mansplaining.

senses: In ancient Athens (and some other cities), the temporary banishment by popular vote of a citizen considered dangerous to the state.
Banishment by some general consent.
Temporary exclusion from a community or society.
ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ὀστρακισμός (ostrakismós, “banishment by means of voting with pot shards”), from ὀστρακίζω (ostrakízō, “ostracize”) + -ισμός (-ismós, “-ism”), from ὄστρακον (óstrakon, “clay pot”).
examples: Witnesse the Ostracisme amongst the Athenians, and the Petalisme among the Siracusans.

senses: A pot, bucket, or basin, in which molten plate glass is carried from the melting pot to the casting table.
A small vessel with at least two flat and transparent sides, used to hold a liquid sample to be analysed in the light path of a spectrometer.
The inner lid of a timepiece.
ety: Borrowed from French cuvette.
examples: The cell / DNA mixtures were nucleoporated in 1 cm transfection cuvettes according to a predefined program on the Nucleofactor.

senses: A host or entertainer.
ety: From Amphitryon, from Ancient Greek Ἀμφιτρύων (Amphitrúōn). So named from the portrayal of Amphitryon in Molière's comedy (itself based on Plautus's) as giving a great dinner.
examples: Our amphitryon emptied into it six bottles of Bordeaux, four of sherry, and two of rum, sweetening and seasoning the whole with sugar and nutmeg.

senses: In the manner of an uncle, pertaining to an uncle.
Kind, genial, benevolent, or tolerant.
ety: From Medieval Latin avunculāris, from Classical Latin avunculus (“maternal uncle”) + -āris (“-ar”).
examples: Both uncle Frank and uncle Stephen Austen had made it a point of principle to be rigorously unsentimental in the discharge of their avuncular obligations.
Bald, obliging, and on his way to training classes for his Irish setter, Mr. Telle is more the portrait of avuncular Norwegian affability than a would-be climate warrior.
But Jackson had an avuncular feeling for the two younger men and he assumed it was his duty to pull them from their gloom.

senses: The assignment of a commercial value to something previously without such value.
The transformation from being commercialized on a nonfungible basis into becoming a commodity that is fungible.
ety: From commodify + -ification.
examples: Subcultures tend to go through continual cycles of commodification and resistance to that commodification.
A company that innovates to achieve the commercialization of a technology often must shift strategy some decades later in response to the advent of that technology's commodification.

senses: Earth which grass has grown into the upper layer of; greensward, sod, turf; (countable) a portion of such earth.
An expanse of land covered in grass; a lawn or meadow.
ety: The noun is derived from Middle English swerd, sward (“rind, skin; leather strap; sod, turf”) [and other forms], from Old English sweard (“rind; skin”), from Proto-Germanic *swarduz (“rind; tough skin; turf”); further etymology unknown. The verb is derived from the noun.
examples: Only where George stood was there left a sward as of yore; the great, level, green lawn that served for both the Major's house and his daughter's.

senses: To engage in or discuss politics.
To give something political characteristics; to turn into a political issue.
To make someone politically active or aware.
ety: From politic + -ize.
examples: My parents started politicizing the weather as soon as they opened their snowplow business.

The possibility of setting up an educational arm which could politicize gays in Massachusetts through a series of seminars and through the publication of a booklet providing a background on the history of gay rights.

senses: A person who owns, plays or practices with the saxophone.
ety: From saxophone + -ist.
examples: They enjoyed music from a live saxophonist during the journey before visiting Braintree Town Hall for refreshments and Christmas cake.
